sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Trengtreng** ​(*trengtreng*) — ‌The Thunder ‌of ​the Mapuche ​— ​belongs to ​the Mapuche ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Flood, ‌Land-Shaping". The ​name means ‌"Mapuche ​thunder and ​war god"[^1].

​**Trengtreng** ​is one ​of ‌the primordial ​volcanic peaks ‌of ​Mapuche cosmology ‌— a ​sacred ‌height raised ​by ‌the earth-serpent ​Trentren above ​the ‌flood-waters of ‌Caicai Vilu. ‌Its ​thunder-name crackles ​like ‌the storms ​that roll ​across ‌the southern ​Andes: with ​its ‌counterpart Kai-Kai ​it ‌embodies the ​living power ​of ​the volcano ​and the ‌sacred ‌geography that ​anchors ‌Mapuche identity.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the ‌name as ‌**Trengtreng** and ‌serves ‌its temple ​at ‌[trengtreng.com](https://trengtreng.com). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*trengtreng* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by ‌the early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for this ​name; **Trengtreng** ​is a ​scholarly transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the name ​means "Mapuche ‌thunder and ​war god"[^1].

‌A Mapuche ​theonym for ‌the thunder-and-war ​god; its ​formation is ​best explained ​as onomatopoeic ​or descriptive ‌within Mapuche ​oral tradition, ‌with no ​known external ‌cognates.

The ​ASCII form ‌*trengtreng* survives ​only because ‌the early ​domain-name system ​could not ‌carry diacritics; ‌it is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ​**Trengtreng** recovers ‌the full ​diacritic detail ​of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— a ‌description computed ‌from the ​displayed form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **t** ‌→ **T** ‌— Same
- ‌**r** → ‌**r** — ​Same
- **e** ‌→ **e** ​— Same
- ​**n** → ​**n** — ‌Same
- **g** ​→ **g** ​— Same
- ​**t** → ‌**t** — ​Same
- **r** ​→ **r** ​— Same
- ‌**e** → ​**e** — ‌Same
- **n** ​→ **n** ‌— Same
- ​**g** → ‌**g** — ‌Same

The ​project holds ​the domain ​**trengtreng.com** (trengtreng.com) ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/tɾeŋˈtɾeŋ/** ​— Mapudungun Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **tɾeŋ** ​— Alveolar ​onset followed by ‌close-mid [e] ​and a ​velar nasal [ŋ]; ‌the first ​syllable of ‌the reduplicated ​thunder name.
- **-** ‌— Reduplication ​divider; the ​name is ​doubled to intensify ​sound and ​power.
- **tɾeŋ** ‌— Repeated ​syllable, producing the ‌rattling, drum-like ​effect of ‌rolling thunder.

​For the modern ‌speaker, the ​closest approximation ‌is: TRENG-TRENG ​— a rattling, ​drum-like reduplication ‌that mimics ‌successive thunderclaps.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms of ​the name:

- ‌**Mapuche serpent-duel** — ​Trentren Vilu, ​the earth-serpent ‌(in some ​records Trengtreng Vilu) ​— his ‌rising hills ​against Caicai ‌Vilu’s rising sea ​raised the ​flood-mountains.
- **Storm-complex** ​— Pillán ​— the thunder-and-volcano ‌spirit in ‌whose storm-world ​the peak’s ‌thunder-name belongs; reduplicated ​treng-treng is ​the sound ‌of his voice.
- ‌**Colonial record** ‌— Treng-treng, ‌recorded by ​Alonso de Ovalle ‌in the ​Histórica Relación ​del Reino ​de Chile (1646).

‌Trengtreng is ​a reduplicated, ​onomatopoeic Mapuche ​name for thunder; ‌reduplication is ​a productive ​device for ​intensification in Mapudungun. ‌Because the ​Latin alphabet ‌renders all ​of its sounds ‌without diacritics, ​the Unicode ‌restoration coincides with ‌the ASCII ​form, so ​the name ​is a plain ​form by ‌tradition rather ‌than by ​restored marks.

sections.body:
**Trengtreng** ​is one ‌of ‌the primordial ​volcanic ​peaks of ​Mapuche ​cosmology — ​a sacred ‌height ​raised by ​the ‌earth-serpent Trentren ​above ‌the flood-waters ​of ‌Caicai Vilu. ​Its ​thunder-name crackles ​like ​the storms ​that ‌roll across ​the southern ‌Andes: ​with its ‌counterpart ​Kai-Kai it ‌embodies ​the living ‌power ​of the ​volcano ‌and the ‌sacred ‌geography that ​anchors ​Mapuche identity.[^1]

### ‌Thunder

The ​reduplicated ​name is ‌onomatopoeic ​for rolling ​thunder; ‌the spirit's ​voice ‌is heard ​in ​storms and ​volcanic ​eruptions.

### Sacred ‌Mountain

Trengtreng ‌is ​one of ‌the ​volcanic peaks ​raised ‌by Pillan ‌to ‌save the ‌people ​from the ‌primordial ​deluge.

### Warrior ​Spirit

​As a ‌thunder-and-war power, ​the ​spirit lends ​Mapuche ‌fighters the ​striking ​force of ​the ‌storm and ​the ‌macana club.

### ​Flood ‌Survivor

Those ​who ‌climbed the ‌sacred peaks ​during ​the flood ​became ​the ancestors ‌of ‌later Mapuche ​communities.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
**Trengtreng** is a sacred ​volcanic peak in Mapuche cosmology, one of ‌the primordial heights raised during the great ‌flood. Together with its counterpart Kai-Kai, it ​embodies the volcanic forces that shaped the ​southern Andes and the sacred geography that ​still anchors Mapuche identity.[^1]

### The Flood and ​the Volcanic Pillars (Flood)

Mapuche tradition tells ​of a primordial deluge driven by Caicai ‌Vilu, the water-serpent, enemy of the earth-serpent Trentren ​and of humankind. As Caicai made the ​sea rise to drown the world, Trentren ‌raised the hills in answer, each power ​straining against the other until the mountains ‌out-topped the waters; the peaks of Trengtreng ​and Kai-Kai became refuges above the flood, ‌while above the serpents stood Pillán, lord ​of volcano and storm. Those who reached ​the heights survived and became the ancestors ​of the Mapuche. The thunder spirit Pillán ​stood above the serpents, lord of volcano ​and storm, lending the earth-serpent his fire. ‌The fullest colonial record of the duel ​is Alonso de Ovalle’s *Histórica Relación* (1646), ‌drawing on Mapuche informants of the Arauco ​frontier. The myth means the Andes themselves ‌are a rescue — the cordillera is not ​scenery but the shape of survival, raised ‌on purpose against the sea.[^2]

### Pillán and ​the Sacred Heights (Theophany)

Pillán, the Mapuche ‌thunder-and-volcano spirit, is the power whose name ​crackles in storms and whose fire runs ​down the cordillera. The voice of the ‌volcano is his voice, its eruption his ‌weapon; the chroniclers describe the thunder spirits ‌waging war from the heights with fire ​and storm. Trengtreng belongs to his storm-world ​twice over — as one of the ‌peaks raised in the flood-duel, and as ​a name that rattles like the thunder ​it imitates — which is why colonial ‌sources sometimes blur the mountain, the thunder-sound, ​and the god into a single figure. ​Later Andean Catholicism read the same volcanoes ‌as signs of divine anger, while Mapuche communities ​kept Pillán in oral tradition and ritual. ‌The myth means a mountain can be ​at once geology and presence: the peak ​is where the sky’s violence touches the ​earth’s.

### The Ancestors on the Heights (Ancestry)

​In the flood narrative the survivors who ‌climbed Trengtreng, Kai-Kai, and the other sacred ‌heights became the ancestors of the later ​communities — so the mountain functions as ‌an origin place, the point where a ​living people connects to a mythic past ​of catastrophe and renewal. The tradition keeps ‌its geography exact and inhabited: the volcanoes ‌of the southern cordillera are named, known, ‌and visited, and oral genealogy runs through ‌them rather than around them. Pilgrimage, storytelling, ​and the everyday toponymy of Araucanía — ‌where mountain names are spoken in Mapudungun, not ​Spanish — keep the peak active in ​Mapuche identity long after the flood has ​receded. The myth means ancestry here is ‌not abstract: it is a specific slope ​you can climb, a horizon you can ​point to from the valley floor.

### The ​Living Mountain (Legacy)

Today Trengtreng remains a ‌landmark of the southern Andean landscape and ​a point of reference in Mapuche oral ​geography. The flood myth survives in several ​colonial witnesses — Alonso de Ovalle’s *Histórica ‌Relación del Reino de Chile* (1646), Pedro ​Mariño de Lobera’s *Crónica del reino de ‌Chile*, and Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo’s *Historia ​de Chile* (1575) — the earliest written ‌records of a far older oral tradition. ​Modern Mapuche writers, musicians, and territorial movements invoke ‌the flood mountains as symbols of resilience ‌and sacred land, and the name endures ​in local toponymy, and the volcano chain ​itself — Llaima, Villarrica, Lonquimay — still ​performs the myth with smoke and tremor. ​The myth means the tradition proved more ‌durable than the empire that wrote it ‌down: the chroniclers’ pages closed, and the ​mountains kept the story.

sections.label: Colonial Chronicles
sections.body:
Colonial chronicles by Spanish and indigenous authors record Trengtreng within the context of indigenous American religion and society. These texts preserve the name after the conquest, often through mediated translation.

The restored form Trengtreng follows normalized Quechua, Aymara, or Mapudungun spelling as appropriate.[^1]

sources.citation: Alonso de Ovalle, Histórica Relación del Reino de Chile (1646).

sections.label: Archaeological Sites
sections.body:
Archaeological sites across the Americas provide material context for the veneration of Trengtreng. Ceramics, textiles, and offerings encode the figure's domain of flood.

The Unicode restoration Trengtreng gives the name a stable modern form alongside the material record.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Trengtreng ​is the ‌myth that ‌looks ​most like ​its own ​landscape. ​A flood-mountain ​raised by ‌a ​serpent against ​the sea ‌explains, ​in one ‌image, why ​the ‌southern Andes ​erupt, why ​the ​coast is ​deadly, and ​why ‌the people’s ​ancestors ‌lived — ​and it ‌does ​so in ‌a grammar ​of ‌height: survive ​by climbing. ​The ‌doubled name ‌is the ‌sound ​of the ​thunder the ‌volcano ​makes; the ​tradition heard ‌the ​mountain before ​it theorized ‌it.

​There is ‌a quiet ​modern ​lesson here ​that the ​chroniclers ‌never intended. ‌The colonial ​writers ‌recorded the ​flood myth ​as ‌a curiosity ‌of the ‌people ‌they were ​conquering; four ‌centuries ​later the ​chronicles are ​footnotes ‌and the ​mountains ​are still ​there — ‌still ​erupting, still ​named in ​Mapudungun. ‌Trengtreng teaches ​that sacred ‌geography ​is the ‌hardest thing ​a ‌colonizer can ‌fail to ​erase: ​you can ​burn the ​temples, ‌but the ‌horizon keeps ​preaching.[^1]
